title: Observability, Cost, and Performance
summary: Instrument model serving with privacy-conscious logs, metrics, traces, alerts, and cost evidence that connect user outcomes to exact model and runtime identities.
objectives: Define observable questions and service objectives before selecting telemetry fields or dashboards.
Correlate requests, model identities, policy outcomes, errors, latency, resource use, and cost without logging unnecessary content or secrets.
Interpret distributions, queueing, saturation, cardinality, sampling, and missing telemetry correctly.
Create actionable alerts, investigation views, retention controls, and evidence that supports tuning, capacity, release, and incident decisions.

sections.title: Start with operational questions and objectives
paragraphs: Write the questions operators must answer: Is the right model serving? Are users receiving valid results? Which slices fail? Where is time spent? What is queued or rejected? Which resource is saturated? Did an update change quality, security, cost, or recovery? Can an incident be scoped and reproduced?

Define indicators and objectives for availability, successful outcomes, policy outcomes, latency distributions, queue time, throughput, rejection, error, recovery, and budget. A dashboard without a decision or owner becomes decorative telemetry.

sections.title: Correlate logs, metrics, traces, events, and exact identities
paragraphs: Use a request or run identifier to connect gateway, adapter, inference server, runtime, tool, policy, and application events. Record service and instance identity, exact model and runtime bundle, route, operation, status, error category, policy disposition, input and output size measures, queue and processing time, resource observations, and release identifier.

OpenTelemetry semantic conventions provide shared names and stability metadata for telemetry concepts. Version the convention and application fields you adopt. Do not assume every generative-AI field is stable or available across runtimes; preserve an application-owned core and explicit adapters.

sections.title: Minimize sensitive content and control telemetry access
paragraphs: Default to metadata and derived measurements rather than raw prompts, responses, retrieved documents, credentials, headers, or personal identifiers. If sampled content is necessary for an approved purpose, minimize, redact, encrypt, restrict access, record consent or authority, set short retention, audit use, and test deletion.

Threat-model telemetry pipelines, collectors, exporters, stores, dashboards, alerts, and support bundles. A secure serving path can still disclose data through verbose errors, traces, exception bodies, labels, exemplars, or high-cardinality identifiers.

sections.title: Measure distributions, saturation, and attributable cost
paragraphs: Record latency and size as distributions with suitable histogram resolution or buckets, not only averages. Prometheus documents that precomputed summary quantiles are generally not aggregatable across replicas, while histograms support later aggregation subject to their representation. Preserve counts, failures, and the population behind every percentile.

Measure queue time, time to first output, processing and streaming time, throughput, cancellations, retries, cache behavior, accelerator and host utilization, memory headroom, storage and network activity, and energy or cloud charges where available. Attribute costs by bounded tenant, workload, route, model, and release without using unbounded labels.

sections.title: Alert on symptoms with actionable context
paragraphs: Alert on user-visible objective burn, critical safety or security outcomes, sustained queueing, rejection, errors, memory pressure, unavailable replicas, model-identity mismatch, telemetry loss, cost anomalies, and failed backup or rollback checks. Attach owner, severity, runbook, evidence links, and safe first actions.

Test alert firing, routing, deduplication, suppression, escalation, and recovery. Preserve baseline and deployment annotations so an operator can compare before and after a change. Missing telemetry is a condition to detect, not evidence that the service is healthy.

activity.title: Build a privacy-conscious observability contract
instructions: Write ten operator questions and map each to signals, exact identities, dimensions, owner, decision, and retention.
Define request, model, release, policy, latency, queue, error, saturation, and cost fields with stability and cardinality limits.
Classify every proposed field as required metadata, optional sensitive content, prohibited secret, or derived measurement.
Design latency and size histograms, objective calculations, and cost allocation for three replicas without averaging quantiles.
Create five alerts and paper-test firing, routing, evidence, runbook, escalation, and recovery.
evidence: An operator-question-to-signal matrix and versioned telemetry field contract.
A privacy, access, retention, redaction, cardinality, sampling, and deletion review.
Objective, distribution, cost, dashboard, and alert fixtures with tested-paper incident and recovery links.

instructorScript.transcript: Begin with user, operator, release, capacity, cost, and incident questions, then define indicators, objectives, owners, and decisions. A dashboard exists to support action. Version an application-owned telemetry core that records exact model and runtime identities while adapting external conventions explicitly. Correlate gateway, adapter, server, runtime, policy, resource, release, and outcome signals with a bounded identifier. Prefer metadata and derived measures, prohibit secrets, and tightly govern any approved content sampling, retention, access, and deletion. Threat-model collectors, exporters, stores, dashboards, alerts, and support bundles. Measure latency, size, queueing, saturation, retries, and cost as attributable distributions with controlled cardinality. Do not average precomputed quantiles across replicas or omit the population and failures. Alert on user-visible objectives and critical controls with owners, runbooks, evidence, escalation, and tested recovery. Detect telemetry loss and preserve deployment annotations so operators can compare a failing release with its verified baseline.

questions.prompt: What should come before dashboard design?
choices: Operational questions, indicators, objectives, owners, and decisions
questions.explanation: Telemetry should answer owned operational questions and support decisions.

questions.prompt: Which identity is essential for release comparison?
choices: Exact model, runtime, configuration, and release identity
questions.explanation: Exact identities connect observed behavior to the build that produced it.

questions.prompt: What is the safest default for prompt and response content in telemetry?
choices: Do not collect it unless an approved minimized and governed use requires it
questions.explanation: Content can contain sensitive data and should not be collected by default.

questions.prompt: Why should latency be recorded as a distribution?
choices: Averages hide tails and populations needed for service decisions
questions.explanation: Tail behavior and population shape matter for users and capacity.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with averaging p95 values from multiple summaries?
choices: Precomputed summary quantiles are generally not aggregatable that way
questions.explanation: Quantiles are not linear values that can generally be averaged across populations.

questions.explanation: An alert must route a meaningful condition into an owned response.
